content: 1. A study conducted in the United States by Jafa et al. (2009) revealed that HIV diagnosis among prison inmates was often delayed due to the lack of testing facilities within prisons. This highlights the critical need for early diagnosis and treatment, as a significant proportion of individuals who seroconverted were infected with drug-resistant strains of HIV. 2. Javanbakht et al. (2007) reported that prevention programs targeting men who have sex with men (MSM) in prison included individual-level HIV education, condom distribution, and counseling for HIV and sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Screening in these programs identified a high prevalence of both HIV and STIs. 3. Beckwith et al. (2010) demonstrated that only 28% of participants in a conventional cohort received their HIV test results, compared to 100% in a rapid testing cohort. Rapid testing significantly improved the likelihood of inmates receiving their results. 4. Macgowan et al. (2009) found that rapid HIV testing in prisons identified a substantial number of previously undiagnosed cases. It also increased the number of prisoners receiving their results and reduced the time required to deliver these results. 5. In South Africa, Motshabi et al. (2011) observed that while most participants were knowledgeable about HIV transmission, barriers to testing and counseling included stigma, discrimination, lack of trust in healthcare professionals, poor attitudes of healthcare staff, and unawareness of voluntary counseling and testing (VCT) services. Programs addressing stigma and discrimination among healthcare workers were recommended. 6. De Voux et al. (2012) reported that HIV testing in jails, as part of the EnhanceLink demonstration project, led to early diagnoses of HIV infections. Rapid turnover of inmates was not a barrier to jail-based HIV screening, but most inmates did not initiate care while detained. Emphasis was placed on linking individuals to care after release. 7. Beckwith et al. (2011) found that staff and key informants preferred rapid HIV testing over conventional methods due to positive experiences. Rapid testing increased compliance among prisoners and reduced staff workload. Immediate access to test results was seen as a major advantage, especially in high-turnover prison populations. 8. Strick et al. (2011) reported that changing testing procedures in Washington State jails from testing upon request to opt-in and then to opt-out testing increased testing rates among inmates from 5% to 72% and then to 90%, respectively. Opt-out testing was the most effective for case detection. 9. Tartar et al. (2012) noted that as part of the testing process, inmates were assured of free medical care during their incarceration and outpatient treatment after release for those without health insurance. Rapid testing increased the number of inmates receiving their results before discharge, and many received their first HIV test while in jail. 10. Tuli et al. (2009) described HIV and syphilis screening and condom distribution programs in the MSM unit of the Los Angeles County Jail. Modeling suggested that these interventions could prevent numerous sexually transmitted infections at low cost and save costs in scenarios where inmates continued sexual activity similar to that outside jail. 11. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), UNAIDS, and WHO (2009) recommended comprehensive HIV prevention programs in prisons, including education, condom and lubricant provision, needle and syringe programs, drug dependence treatment, and access to antiretroviral therapy (ART). Evidence showed that ART significantly reduced mortality due to HIV/AIDS in countries where it was accessible, including among incarcerated individuals. 12. Roberson et al. (2009) identified barriers to ART adherence in prisons, including lack of confidentiality, stigma, limited access to medication, and strained relationships with prison health staff. Recommendations included involving inmates in program design, protecting medical information, and improving relationships between providers and inmates. 13. Fontana et al. (2007) highlighted the lack of continuity of care between prison and community settings during the release period. Improved discharge models were recommended to enhance collaboration between prison systems and community healthcare providers, increasing retention in care. 14. Small et al. (2009) in Canada noted delays in obtaining HIV care and treatment in prisons. Poor relationships between prison health staff and inmates, high levels of stigma, and challenges in ensuring continuity of treatment post-release negatively impacted adherence. 15. Shalihu et al. (2014) in Namibia identified barriers to ART adherence, including insufficient privacy, stigma, lack of adherence support, poor nutrition, discrimination by prison staff, and lack of information about HIV transmission and care. 16. Wohl et al. (2011) found that an intensive case management intervention spanning incarceration and release was as effective as comprehensive pre-release discharge planning in ensuring access to medical care for HIV-infected individuals post-release. 17. Nunn et al. (2010) reported that the COMPASS program, an intensive case management initiative, improved linkage to HIV care and other services for HIV-positive jail inmates in Rhode Island. Participants noted that the program helped prevent drug relapse and facilitated access to housing, mental health care, and addiction services. 18. Catz et al. (2011) emphasized the need for confidential delivery of HIV prevention information in prisons to reduce stigma and safety threats. Timely updates on HIV prevention and care should be provided in a manner that protects individuals' HIV status. 19. Pant Pai et al. (2009) demonstrated that continuous ART therapy in jail improved CD4 cell counts and viral load control compared to intermittent or no ART. However, intermittent ART was still associated with slower CD4 cell loss compared to no ART. 20. Needle and syringe exchange programs (NSPs) in prisons were found to be feasible and effective in reducing needle-sharing and HIV transmission. Additional benefits included reduced overdose risk and abscesses, as well as increased referrals to drug dependence treatment programs. There was no convincing evidence of major unintended negative consequences. 21. Milloy et al. (2013) in Canada found that viral loads increased during incarceration due to hesitancy to disclose HIV status, treatment interruptions, and delays. Drug use continued in jail, reinforcing the need for needle exchange programs. 22. Seal et al. (2008) reported that inmates often did not use HIV prevention measures when injecting drugs, supporting the need for needle exchange and education programs. 23. Moller et al. (2008) in Kyrgyzstan observed that needle-sharing decreased from 20% to 8% after implementing a needle exchange program in two prisons. 24. Roshanfekr et al. (2013) in Iran found that harm reduction services, including needle exchange programs, significantly reduced drug abuse among prisoners. 25. Studies on condom distribution in prisons, such as those by Sylla et al. (2010) and Butler et al. (2013), showed no evidence that condoms increased sexual activity in prisons but did promote safer sex practices.
